transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-11-05 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~72 minutes
Attendees: Avery Cole (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Lopez (OptimaSearch), Ben Richards (OptimaSearch SRE), Priya Nair (OptimaSearch Product)
Shared items: sample traffic script link (customer), Redwood POC checklist (drive.redwood/POC-4829), benchmark harness config template (redwood.app/harness-templates)

Summary: Quick scoping call to align on POC acceptance criteria and the harness integration approach. Main discussion points: define throughput windows, KV cache warmup strategy (prefix caching), decide streaming vs non-streaming for their client, and agree on telemetry/metrics (p95/p99, cold-starts). Action items and dates captured at end.

Transcript:
[00:00] Avery: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, can you all hear me?
[00:02] Maya: Yep, loud and clear.
[00:05] Ben: Good here.
[00:10] Avery: Great. Quick intros, I am Avery, AE at Redwood. Samir is our SE, he runs the benchmark harness normally. Samir, want to intro?
[00:18] Samir: Sure, hi, I'm Samir Patel, I do a lot of the load testing and the kv-cache warmup scripts, also routing/fallback stuff.
[00:26] Maya: Maya Lopez, lead ML eng at OptimaSearch. We own the scoring pipeline.
[00:29] Ben: Ben Richards, infra/SRE. I'll handle network and perf counters.
[00:33] Priya: Priya Nair, product, driving timeline and success criteria.
[00:37] Avery: Cool. Objective - scope a POC showing we can meet OptimaSearch's throughput and tail-latency targets using your real scripts. We want to agree on which model family, the traffic shape, and the warmup approach so the harness runs are representative.
[00:50] Priya: For business context: we need to serve a live product demo to sales in early December, and if the POC looks good we will talk Dedicated pools. So timeline's tight.
[00:58] Avery: Understood. We're thinking a short 48-hour pilot to show steady-state and spike resilience.
[01:05] Maya: Quick technical note: our traffic is 60% short prompts (~40 tokens) and 40% long prompts (~800 tokens), the long ones happen in bursts tied to batched scoring jobs. Also we do session-based caching (prefix reuse) heavily.
[01:20] Samir: That distribution is great to test both KV hit-rate and generation load. A key question: do you want streaming responses for the long prompts or is non-streaming ok? Streaming reduces perceived latency but changes client-side throughput characteristics.
[01:33] Priya: For the demo we prefer streaming so UI shows tokens as they arrive, but for the batch scoring jobs non-streaming is simpler.
[01:40] Ben: Our runner currently uses a single client adapter that expects full responses; modifying to streaming will need some client work but it's doable. We'll scope how much effort.
[01:48] Avery: Ok so POC should cover both modes—streaming for interactive flows, non-streaming for batch. We'll capture both in the harness and report separate metrics.
[01:57] Maya: Success criteria first — from product: interactive p95 under 400ms for short prompts and p99 under 1s for long streaming shortest-first? Wait, that phrasing might be off. We want perceived latency low for short calls and p99 for long calls sub 3s.
[02:15] Samir: Let me restate so we have clean metrics: short prompt SLOs — p95 < 400 ms, p99 < 900 ms measured end-to-end; long prompt SLOs — median token latency acceptable, and full completion p99 < 3s for streaming UI or under 5s for non-streaming in batch. Also throughput target around steady 150 RPS with 500 RPS spikes. Does that align?
[02:36] Priya: Yes, 150 steady and spike to 500 for 5-10 minutes.
[02:42] Ben: On infra we want to ensure cold-starts don't blow p99. We care about KV cache warmup because our long prompts reuse prefixes a lot, if KV cache cold we see 5x token costs.
[02:53] Samir: Right — we'll implement a warmup window where we pre-seed KV with common prefix sequences before the main test. The harness supports an initial 'warmup' phase — we typically do 10-30 minutes of scripted warmups depending on dataset size. For your workload I'd recommend an adaptive warmup: start with 15 minutes and measure KV-hit ratio, then extend if hits < 80%.
[03:13] Maya: How do you simulate real prefix reuse? Our prefixes include user context + 2-3 system messages, some variable tokens.
[03:21] Samir: We run the exact customer scripts you provide; the harness supports session stickiness and will replay the same prefixes so the runtime's KV gets populated. If you want paranoia-level fidelity, we can run a parallel pass using a high-fidelity recorder that replays cached tokens exactly.
[03:35] Maya: We'll share the script tarball. Note: some PII gets scrubbed, hope the recorder won't need raw PII.
[03:42] Samir: We don't need raw PII — sanitized inputs are fine. We just need stable tokenization.
[03:47] Ben: Questions on streaming vs non-streaming: does streaming materially change token emission timing and hence tail latency numbers?
[03:54] Samir: It does. Streaming reduces perceived latency but can increase backend pressure since there are more frequent small writes. For p99 latency it's often better but throughput accounting differs. We'll capture both: per-token latency and time-to-first-byte.
[04:06] Priya: OK. What about batching? you mentioned batch sizes earlier.
[04:10] Samir: Yes, batching impacts cost and latency. For low-latency interactive traffic, we'll configure small dynamic batching (N=4-8) with a 5-10ms scheduling window. For batch scoring we operate at larger batch sizes (N=16-64) to optimize throughput. Harness will run the two profiles separately.
[04:24] Maya: Does Redwood runtime support per-route batching configs? We route interactive and batch through same endpoint but with different priority.
[04:31] Samir: We can create two routes, yes—interactive route with aggressive latency SLOs and smaller batch windows, batch route with larger windows and preemptive pooling. That's part of the POC config.
[04:43] Ben: We need to see exact CPU/GPU utilization traces and token cost estimates during the run. Can you export that?
[04:48] Samir: Yes, the harness captures token-level cost, GPU utilization, memory, and per-request trace ids. We'll export a CSV and a dashboard link.
[04:56] Priya: For acceptance: besides latency targets, we want cost-per-1M tokens under a threshold — can you provide a preliminary estimate?
[05:04] Avery: We'll provide a pricing ballpark after we pick model & quantization. But Samir can show measured token-rate and we can estimate. Note that Dedicated vs Hosted changes unit economics.
[05:15] Maya: On model choice: we plan to test a 13B open model (opt-13b-like) and a quantized 4-bit variant. The runtime must be able to fallback to a smaller model if capacity constrained.
[05:27] Samir: We will include model variants and test fallback behavior: simulate a constrained pool and validate graceful degradation (increase latency but maintain throughput, or route to cheaper model). We'll log model-switch events.
[05:37] Maya: For the warmup we need to measure KV-hit ratio behavior over time. Can you plot that?
[05:42] Samir: Yes, KV hit-rate vs time, plus token-per-request and p50/p95/p99 curves.
[05:47] Ben: Network: we'll need outbound ports allowed to redwood test IPs. I'll send a list. Also want to ensure the harness can run from our VPC to mimic on-prem network.
[05:56] Avery: We can either run harness from our Redwood-hosted runners or run a local harness in your VPC — for fidelity we recommend running the client adapter inside your network so network path is representative.
[06:06] Ben: We'll run it in our VPC. I'll need the runner binary and a config.
[06:10] Samir: We'll hand over a Dockerized client adapter and a small orchestration script. It binds to your sample dataset and streams telemetry back to the dashboard.
[06:18] Priya: Timeline recap?
[06:20] Avery: Customer to send scripts by 2027-11-10. We will prepare harness and run the 48-hour pilot starting 2027-11-11, results review on 2027-11-12 (quick sync) and full report/next-steps the following week.
[06:32] Maya: Sounds good. A couple of wrinkles: some of our long prompts include function-calling style structured outputs. Does the harness record function-call tokenization interactions?
[06:40] Samir: Yes — we support function/tool calling and will log structured outputs and any token-duplication issues. We sometimes see increased token counts due to repeated tool output; we can measure that.
[06:50] Ben: On monitoring, we want to map request IDs back to our logs. Does the harness support custom trace IDs?
[06:56] Samir: We can accept a client-provided trace id header and propagate it, so you can join traces.
[07:02] Priya: Any blockers on your side for the 11/11 run?
[07:06] Samir: Not really. We need the canonical scripts and confirmation that running sanitized samples in our test harness is OK. Also Ben's firewall rules and the VPC runner access.
[07:15] Ben: I'll get the firewall and a short RDP-ish access plan.
[07:19] Maya: Regarding acceptance: can we get a pass/fail rubric? We want a checklist that product/SRE can sign off on.
[07:26] Avery: We'll send a POC acceptance checklist that includes: throughput windows met (150 steady / 500 spike), SLO latency buckets for short and long prompts, KV cache hit-rate >= 80% after warmup, graceful fallback verified, and cost-per-1M tokens estimate within threshold.
[07:40] Priya: Good. Also include an item for security/compliance — we need an audit log of test runs.
[07:45] Samir: The runtime emits audit logs; we'll provide those and mask PII.
[07:50] Maya: Fine. A small nit: when you say 'p99 < 3s for long streaming' that's aggressive for 800-token prompts if we include generation time. Are you counting time-to-first-token or total generation?
[08:00] Samir: Good call. We'll separate metrics: time-to-first-byte (TTFB) and time-to-completion. We'll record both and align the SLOs accordingly.
[08:08] Ben: Anything about retries? Do you have transient errors during spikes?
[08:12] Samir: We'll simulate error-injection and verify retry/backoff behavior. The harness can inject 5% error at spike boundaries to test fallback routes.
[08:20] Priya: Ok let's capture next steps and owners.
[08:23] Avery: Recap: Maya will send scripts and sample prompts by 11/10; Ben will provide firewall/IPs and confirm VPC runner access; Samir will prepare the warmup plan and harness config; Avery will send POC checklist and pricing sketch. We'll run pilot 11/11-11/12 and review 11/12.
[08:40] Maya: One last question — for KV cache warmup, can we do progressive warmup per session, or do you only do global pre-seeding?
[08:48] Samir: Both. We support global pre-seed and session-local progressive warmup. For high-fidelity we'll pre-seed common prefixes then allow session warmup to adapt.
[08:58] Ben: Thanks everyone.
[09:00] Avery: Thanks, we'll follow up with the docs and the runbook.
[09:03] Priya: Thanks.
[09:05] Meeting ended.
